props.title: The Last Metro
props.initialSlug: Theater fights Nazi occupation in wartime Paris

sections.content: The Last Metro stands as François Truffaut's masterful examination of art, resistance, and survival during Nazi-occupied France. Set in a Parisian theater, the film weaves together the story of Marion Steiner (Catherine Deneuve) running her Jewish husband's theater while hiding him in the basement. Truffaut, unlike his earlier New Wave works like The 400 Blows (1959), adopts a more classical narrative style here, drawing parallels with Ernst Lubitsch's To Be or Not to Be (1942) in its portrayal of theater as both escape and resistance.

sections.content: The film's claustrophobic atmosphere mirrors works like Le Corbeau (1943), made during the actual occupation. Truffaut masterfully uses the theater setting as a metaphor for the larger deception required to survive - actors playing roles both on and off stage. The relationship between Marion and Bernard Granger (Gérard Depardieu) develops against this backdrop of artifice and authenticity, recalling the complex moral choices depicted in Lacombe, Lucien (1974).

What sets The Last Metro apart is its focus on cultural resistance rather than armed conflict. Like Jules and Jim (1962), Truffaut explores love triangles and human relationships, but here they're framed by survival rather than romance. The film's technical brilliance shows in its use of warm theater lighting contrasting with the cold exterior world, reminiscent of Day for Night (1973), Truffaut's other great film about filmmaking. sections.content: The film's exploration of theater as resistance connects to broader themes in French cinema about art during wartime. Like Marcel Carné's Children of Paradise (1945), filmed during the occupation, The Last Metro shows how art becomes both shelter and weapon. The basement scenes, where Lucas Steiner (Heinz Bennent) directs by proxy, echo the real-life stories of artists who continued working in secret during the occupation, similar to the underground filmmaking depicted in Inglourious Basterds (2009).
